title: Sin is behovely (ch. 27)
hookLine: sin was necessary, she says, but all shall be well
tomorrow: what if you fall while you're running to help?

cards: It's the question that turns up at two in the morning, at a hospital bedside, in the comments under a hard headline. If God is good and able, why not stop the bad thing before it starts?
Julian of Norwich asks it straight out, about sin itself. The answer she receives doesn't explain as much as it promises.

teach.b: In chapter twenty-seven, Julian wonders why God, in his great wisdom, didn't prevent sin's beginning. Then, she thinks, all would have been well.
The first half of the answer: sin is behovely. It's an old English word readers gloss as fitting, or needed, something with its place. She doesn't call sin good.
She says she never saw sin itself; it has no substance of its own, and she knew it only by the pain it causes.

teach.h: ALL SHALL BE WELL, SAID TENDERLY.
teach.b: The second half, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." She isn't told how.

And he says it, she writes, very tenderly, with no blame toward her, nor toward any who will be saved. A promise said more than once, to someone weighed down, is something another tradition knows too.
In the Qur'an, a short surah speaks to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and repeats itself.
In Pickthall's translation: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." Muslims receive those words as God's own. Here's the honest difference.

The surah speaks of hardship and the ease that comes with it. Julian's promise is about sin itself, and for her it's Jesus who speaks it. Two different voices, each repeating the promise so it can be heard.

how: Some Catholics pray with Julian's 'all shall be well' in times of worry; her book is read as devotion, alongside the Church's teaching on sin and redemption.

o: sin is beyond God's reach to ever mend
sin is harmless and needs no forgiveness
sin has a fitting place, yet all will be well

games.q: sin is behovely — tap the pairs.
p: with hardship goeth ease, said twice

s: all shall be well means nothing bad will happen to you
Julian holds the pain of sin as real. it's a promise about the end, not a forecast for this week.
she is told exactly how all will be made well
it's a promise, not an explanation; she isn't told how.
she says the words were spoken tenderly, with no blame toward her
chapter 27: no blame to her, nor to any who will be saved.

games.q: your friend's little sister asks why God lets people do bad things if he could stop them. you want to give Julian's answer honestly. which fits?
o: Julian asked that too. she was told sin has its place and all shall be well, but not how.
Julian proved that sin is actually good for us, so it doesn't matter.
Julian said nobody is allowed to ask God a question like that.
games.why: Julian asked the same question, got a promise instead of an explanation, and heard it said tenderly. honest, and kind to a child.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one failure you still carry. Don't argue for it or against it; set Julian's line beside it, all shall be well, and leave the how alone.
Anyone who prays can hand that one thing to God until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Sin is behovely. Julian's hard word: sin has its place, and still all shall be well.

carryVoice: Your line: all manner of thing. Not some things, but all manner of thing shall be well. Sleep well.
